title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, and ADRs
author: Asha Patel
body:
Overview:

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's architecture and engineering standards across API design, coding practices, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, performance, and the ADR (Architecture Decision Record) process. It is intended to be a single-source reference for engineers, product managers, and architects when designing services or making infra and runtime decisions.

Scope:
- Public REST/HTTP APIs and internal service-to-service RPCs
- Server and runtime code that powers hosted, dedicated, and private deployments
- Deployment and infra configuration (cloud and on-prem packaging)
- Model-serving runtime and compilation decisions
- Observability, SLOs, and performance measurement
- ADR process and canonical decision templates

Principles:
1. Consistency: APIs, telemetry, and deployment patterns must be consistent across teams to reduce cognitive load and enable predictable operations.
2. Production-first: Optimize for latency, reliability, cost, and debuggability in that order for customer-facing inference paths.
3. Ownership: Every service and ADR must have a clear owner and rollback plan.
4. Replaceability: Components should be swappable (e.g., model variant, quantization profile) without customer-visible changes when possible.

1) API Standards

Purpose: Ensure APIs are discoverable, versioned, secure, and easy to integrate for SDKs and customers.

API design checklist (MUST):
- Use RESTful semantics over HTTP for public endpoints; internal services may use gRPC where low latency and strong typing are required.
- Stable URL patterns: /v{major}/{resource}/{id} (major version in path), e.g., /v1/models/{model_id}/infer.
- Backwards-compatible changes only in patch releases; breaking changes require major version bump and ADR.
- Pagination: use limit/offset for list endpoints only for admin APIs; for large result sets use cursor-based pagination with opaque cursors.
- Idempotency: write operations must accept an Idempotency-Key header and persist deduplication keys for at least 24 hours.
- Authentication: All public APIs require bearer tokens. Private deployments must support token-based and mTLS authentication.
- Rate limiting: return 429 with X-RateLimit-* headers. Annex: rate limit tiers are defined in product-docs/pricing-and-packaging.

API response conventions:
- Successful responses use HTTP 200/201 with a top-level JSON object: {"data": ..., "meta": {...}}.
- Errors use a structured envelope: {"error": {"code": "INVALID_INPUT", "message": "...", "details": [...]}} and map to appropriate 4xx/5xx codes.

2) Coding Standards

Purpose: Maintain readable, secure, and maintainable code across services.

High-level rules:
- Languages: primary service languages are Go (control plane), Rust (runtime hot paths), and Python (evals and tooling). Use language-specific linters and formatters.
- Mandatory linters and formatting: gofmt/golangci-lint for Go, rustfmt/clippy for Rust, black/flake8 for Python.
- Error handling: prefer explicit error returns; attach context for all errors that cross service boundaries.
- Secrets: never hard-code secrets. Use KMS-backed secret injection; local dev secrets must be stored in the dev vault.
- Tests: unit tests required for all code; integration tests for public interfaces. Aim for >60% coverage on business logic; CI gate enforces tests and static analysis.

Style checklist (MUST):
- Small functions (<= 80 lines preferred), clear interfaces, dependency inversion for side-effecting code (I/O, time).
- Use feature flags for behavioral changes expected to be toggled during rollout.
- Document public packages and exported functions with clear examples.

3) Infrastructure Standards

Purpose: Ensure deployments are repeatable, secure, and observable across hosted, dedicated, and private modes.

Configuration and IaC:
- All infra is defined in Terraform modules under eng-infra/terraform-and-iac and must be reviewed via the company CI pipeline.
- Environment parity: dev -> staging -> prod manifests must differ only in parameter values (secrets, capacity).
- Networking: default services run in private subnets; public-facing gateways are behind managed load balancers and WAF.

Security & compliance:
- KMS for all customer key material; HSM available for enterprise/private deployments.
- Audit logging enabled for control plane actions with 365-day retention for enterprise customers, 30 days for hosted by default.

SLA and capacity guidelines:
- Production control plane: 99.95% monthly uptime.
- Dedicated GPU pools: target 99.9% uptime for reserved capacity.
- Autoscaling: thresholds must be explicit in runbooks; burst windows documented per-customer.

Example infra requirement table:
| Component | Minimum Region Setup | Encryption | Owner |
|----------|----------------------|------------|-------|
| Control plane | 3 AZs per region | KMS at-rest & TLS in-transit | eng-platform |
| Serving runtime | GKE/EC2 autoscaled GPU pools | Disk encryption + memory encryption flags | eng-serving-runtime |

4) Model-serving standards

Purpose: Provide consistent expectations for model packaging, quantization, kernel selection, and runtime constraints.

Model packaging and onboarding:
- Models must include a metadata manifest: {"model_id","version","architecture","tokenizer_spec","quantization_candidates"}.
- Provide eval asset bundle with representative prompt-set and expected regression thresholds.
- Quantization profiles (int8/4bit) must be accompanied by quality regression measurements (perplexity and output evals).

Runtime constraints and interfaces:
- Standardized infer contract: Accepts {input, max_tokens, stop, temperature, top_p, stream}. Truncation must be deterministic and documented.
- KV cache format versioned; backward-compatible reads supported for one minor release.
- Kernel selection: runtime may choose optimized kernels based on sequence length histogram; document fallback kernels in model manifest.

Operational controls:
- Per-model throttles and concurrency limits configurable at route level.
- Automatic fallback policy: if a model variant cannot meet latency SLOs, route to a lower-quality (but compatible) variant with gradual traffic shifting.

5) Observability standards

Purpose: Provide consistent telemetry for debugging, alerting, and cost analysis.

Metrics (minimum):
- Request-level: request_latency_ms (p50,p95,p99), request_tokens, request_size_bytes, response_tokens.
- System-level: gpu_utilization, memory_rss_bytes, kv_cache_hit_rate, batch_size_distribution.
- Business-level: cost_per_1k_tokens, requests_per_customer_per_minute.

Tracing and logs:
- Distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry; propagate traceparent and baggage.
- Structured JSON logs with fields: timestamp, service, env, level, request_id, model_id, user_id (hashed), message.
- Sampling: full traces for errors and 1% for successful requests by default; adjustable per-service.

Alerting and SLOs:
- Service SLOs must be defined in the service owner's runbook. Canonical inference SLO: latency p95 <= 150ms for interactive routes (hosted tier) and p95 <= 500ms for batch routes.
- Error budget: rolling 30-day budget; burn rate policies trigger paged alerts when >4x burn for 1 hour.

6) Performance standards and benchmarking

Purpose: Ensure predictable throughput and cost across deployments.

Benchmarking practices:
- Use the central benchmarking suite under eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite. Benchmarks must include representative sequence length distributions and token-rate mixes.
- Measure: latency (p50/p95/p99), throughput (tokens/sec), GPU memory use, and CPU overhead per request.
- Regression policy: any performance regression >5% on latency or >10% on throughput vs baseline requires a regression ADR and can trigger rollout hold.

Optimization guidelines:
- Use continuous batching with adaptive windowing; prefer latency-first batching for interactive routes.
- Cache prefixes aggressively for high-reuse routes and include cache TTL semantics in model route configs.

7) ADR process and templates

When to write an ADR:
- Breaking API changes, infra topology changes, compilation/runtime kernel swaps, and any cross-team contract decisions.

ADRs must include (canonical template):
1. Title
2. Status (proposed | accepted | deprecated)
3. Context and problem statement
4. Considered alternatives (with pros/cons)
5. Decision and rationale
6. Migration plan and rollback steps
7. Owners and review date
8. Related ADRs and implementation tickets

ADR lifecycle rules:
- Draft ADRs must be reviewed by at least two reviewers from affected teams.
- Accepted ADRs are published in this directory and referenced in related service README(s).
- Deprecation: ADRs should include an obsolescence review date (typically 12 months).

8) Ownership and governance

- Engineering architecture guild coordinates cross-cutting standards and reviews ADRs quarterly.
- Service owners are responsible for aligning with these standards and keeping runbooks up-to-date.
- Exceptions require an explicit risk-and-exceptions record and an owner.

Appendix A — Example ADR summary table:
| ADR ID | Title | Status | Owner | Link |
|--------|-------|--------|-------|------|
| ADR-2026-001 | API versioning semantics | accepted | Asha Patel | /confluence/architecture-and-standards/adr-2026-001-api-versioning |
| ADR-2026-007 | Quantization default profile | proposed | Lin Zhao | /confluence/architecture-and-standards/adr-2026-007-quant-profile |

Appendix B — Example runbook checklist for infra changes:
1. Create Terraform plan and open PR.
2. Run CI and integration tests in staging.
3. Announce maintenance window to infra-announce.
4. Perform rolling deploy with canary on 5% traffic.
5. Monitor SLOs for 30 minutes, if anomaly revert.
6. Gradually increase traffic and close change.
